title: Everyday holiness (Chullin)
hookLine: the tractate on ordinary meat sits in the order of holy things
last: LEARNING THE OFFERING COUNTS AS BRINGING IT.

cards: Chullin. The word means ordinary things: not dedicated, not for the altar. Just food.
The chicken for a Friday night dinner, the beef in a weekday stew.
A whole tractate of the Mishnah covers it: how an animal is slaughtered for eating at home, which creatures may be eaten, how meat and milk are kept apart. And here's the odd part.
The Mishnah doesn't file it with the blessings over food. It puts it right in the middle of the order of holy things, beside the Temple's offerings.

teach.b: Everyday holiness. Start with the placement. The Mishnah could have filed ordinary meat anywhere.
It set it down among the offerings. One way to read that: the care given to the altar now follows the food home.

The same attention, the same rules about how an animal dies, apply at a kitchen table. Second, the kitchen itself. The Torah's line is short, in the old JPS translation: "Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk."
From that line, which the Torah gives more than once, the Mishnah and the Talmud build the separation of meat and milk, a chapter of Chullin and much more after it. Third, the ending.
The last chapter of Chullin is about a bird's nest.

teach.h: IT ENDS WITH THE MOTHER BIRD.
teach.b: Deuteronomy says that if you come upon a nest with the mother sitting on the young or the eggs, you let the mother go before you take them.
So the tractate on everyday meat ends with an animal mother, and a law that asks for restraint at the moment you could take everything.
The Mishnah's closing lines reason from it: if a light commandment like this carries the promise of a long life, how much more the weighty ones. Fourth, the table.

teach.h: THE TABLE IN PLACE OF THE ALTAR.
teach.b: With the Temple gone, a teaching in the Talmud says, a person's table atones for them, the way the altar once did. So the order of holy things makes a quiet claim.
Holiness isn't only in the sanctuary. It's in how you slaughter, how you cook, what you leave, and who you feed.

how: Jews who keep kosher follow the laws of slaughter and of separating meat and milk developed from tractate Chullin; others keep some of these customs or none, and some Jewish homes treat the Shabbat table as a place of blessing and welcome.

o: the altar's care brought home to ordinary food
the tractate on animals offered on the Temple altar
the blessing a priest gives at the end of each day

p: let go before the young are taken
atones as the altar once did

s: the tractate on ordinary meat sits in the order of holy things
the Mishnah files Chullin among the Temple offerings.
the Torah spells out every rule of keeping meat and milk apart
the verse is one line. the Mishnah and Talmud build the detailed rules from it.
Chullin ends with a law about a bird's nest
its last chapter is the mother bird, let go before the young are taken.

games.q: you come upon a bird's nest by the road, the mother sitting on the eggs. you want the eggs. what does Deuteronomy say?
o: take the mother and the eggs together.
let the mother go first, then take the eggs.
you may never take from a nest.
games.why: the Torah says to let the mother go. the Mishnah's tractate on ordinary meat ends with this law of restraint.

practice: Think ahead to the next thing you'll eat, a sandwich, leftovers, cereal at the counter, and trace it back for a moment: a field, an animal, a truck, a pair of hands at a register.
Then choose one small way to set that meal apart: sit down for it, put the phone in another room, or share it. If you say a blessing over food, you can plan to say it slowly.

wordCard.voice: Everyday holiness. The tractate Chullin, on ordinary meat, filed in the order of holy things: the altar's care brought home to the table. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: ordinary, unconsecrated things; the tractate on meat eaten at home.

carryVoice: Your line: everyday holiness. In this order, ordinary food was never the opposite of holy. See you tomorrow.
